input:
## Start-up

Before the motor is started, it is essential to ensure that the pump casing and the suction line have been completely filled with liquid. The vent located at the top of the casing should be opened and left open until such time as liquid, free from air, emerges from it, after which it should be closed again. It should be noted that a pump which is started with air present in the casing will fail to develop pressure, and dry running will cause damage to the seals. The suction valve should be confirmed as fully open, and the discharge valve should be confirmed as closed. A check should be made that the coupling guard is in place and that nothing is resting against the rotating parts. The oil level in the bearing housing should be checked at the sight glass, and topped up with the specified oil in the event that the level is found to be low. Where access permits, the shaft should be turned by hand in order to confirm that it rotates freely. The motor should then be bumped and the direction of rotation checked against the arrow marked on the casing; if the rotation is found to be incorrect, the electrical connections must be corrected before any further steps are taken. The motor may then be started, and the discharge valve opened slowly until a flow has been established. The discharge pressure should be observed as the valve is opened, and it will be seen to rise to the duty value as the flow builds up. While the pressure is rising, the seals and casing joints should be checked for leakage, and attention should be paid to any noise emanating from the casing. If the discharge pressure fails to rise, the pump should be stopped immediately and the priming step repeated, since the most usual cause is air that has been left in the casing or in the suction line.

## Normal operation

The pump should be run at its duty point, and the operating conditions should be maintained as steady as possible. At each operating round, the suction pressure, the discharge pressure, and the flow should be read and the readings entered into the log. These readings constitute the record against which subsequent changes are judged, and a drift in any one of them represents the earliest indication that a fault is developing. It is of particular importance that the suction pressure be kept up, since a falling suction pressure brings the pump ever closer to cavitation, a phenomenon which erodes the impeller and significantly shortens its working life. The suction valve must never be throttled in order to control the flow; flow control is to be exercised at the discharge valve. The pump should not be run against a closed discharge valve for longer than the short period permitted at start-up, because the liquid contained within the casing becomes heated when no flow is passing through it. The bearing housing temperature should be checked, by means of the fitted instrument or by hand, at each round, and a housing which is hotter than its usual state should be reported. The seal leakage should also be checked: a small degree of leakage at a packed gland is perfectly normal, whereas a dry gland or a sudden increase in leakage is not. The motor cooling passages should be kept clear and the pump base kept free of spilled liquid. Any abnormal noise, vibration, or burnt smell from the motor should be reported immediately, and the pump should be taken out of service where the fault lies in the rotating parts.

## Alarms

Two alarms are fitted to the pump, and each of them calls for a specific response on the part of the operator. The low suction pressure alarm sounds when the suction pressure falls below its set point. A loss of suction pressure indicates a loss of supply or a loss of prime, and continued running under such conditions will cavitate and damage the impeller. When this alarm sounds, the pump must be stopped. The level in the suction vessel should be checked, the suction line and the strainer should be checked for blockage, and the supply should be restored. The pump must be primed once again before it is restarted, and the underlying cause of the loss should be identified before the pump is returned to service. The high bearing temperature alarm sounds when the bearing housing temperature rises above its set point. A hot bearing is indicative of a lubrication fault or of an overloaded bearing, and continued running will result in the destruction of the bearing. When this alarm sounds, the pump must be stopped and left stopped. The bearings should be allowed to cool. The oil level and the condition of the oil should be checked, and the fault should be reported. The pump must not be restarted until such time as the cause has been found and cleared.

## Shutdown

In order to shut the pump down, the discharge valve should be closed gradually so as to bring the flow down, and the motor should be stopped when the valve is nearly shut. The suction valve should be closed after the motor has stopped. Where a pump is to stand idle, it should be drained at the casing drain if the pumped liquid would otherwise set, corrode the internals, or freeze, and the drainings should be directed to the drain system appropriate to the liquid concerned. Where the pump is to return to service directly and the liquid is stable within the casing, it should be left full. Before any work is carried out on the pump, it must be isolated electrically and the starter tagged, and the isolation must be proven before the work is allowed to start. In summary, this chapter has covered the running of the pump from start to finish: the priming and starting procedure, the readings and checks which form part of normal operation, the two alarms together with the action that each of them calls for, and the shutdown procedure which leaves the pump stopped, isolated, and ready either for work or for its next start.

## Start-up

Confirm that the suction vessel holds enough liquid for the start and that the suction line draws on a filled section of the vessel. Confirm that the pump casing and the suction line are filled with liquid before the motor is started. Open the vent at the top of the casing and leave it open until liquid, free of air, comes from it, then close the vent. A pump started with air in the casing does not develop pressure, and running dry damages the seals. Confirm that the suction valve is fully open and that the discharge valve is closed. Check that the coupling guard is in place and that nothing rests against the rotating parts. Check the oil level in the bearing housing at the sight glass and top up with the specified oil where the level is low. Turn the shaft by hand where access allows and confirm that it rotates freely. Bump the motor and check the direction of rotation against the arrow on the casing; correct the electrical connections before proceeding if the rotation is wrong. Start the motor and open the discharge valve slowly until flow is established. Watch the discharge pressure as the valve opens. The pressure rises to the duty value as the flow builds. Check the seals and the casing joints for leakage while the pressure rises, and listen for noise from the casing. Stop the pump at once if the discharge pressure does not rise, and return to the priming step: the usual cause is air left in the casing or in the suction line.

## Normal operation

Run the pump at its duty point and keep the operating conditions steady. Read the suction pressure, the discharge pressure, and the flow at each operating round and enter the readings in the log. Take the readings at the same points on each round, so that one round can be compared directly with the rounds before it. The readings are the record against which later changes are judged, and a drift in any of them is the first sign of a fault developing. Keep the suction pressure up: a falling suction pressure brings the pump toward cavitation, which erodes the impeller and shortens its life. Never throttle the suction valve to control flow. Control the flow at the discharge valve. Do not run the pump against a closed discharge valve beyond the short period allowed at start-up, because the liquid in the casing heats when no flow passes. Check the bearing housing temperature by the fitted instrument or by hand at each round, and report a housing that is hotter than its usual state. Check the seal leakage: a small leakage at a packed gland is normal, and a dry gland or a sudden increase in leakage is not. Keep the motor cooling passages clear and the pump base free of spilled liquid. Report abnormal noise, vibration, or a burnt smell from the motor at once, and take the pump out of service where the fault is in the rotating parts.

## Alarms

Two alarms are fitted to the pump. The low suction pressure alarm sounds when the suction pressure falls below its set point. Loss of suction pressure means loss of supply or loss of prime, and continued running cavitates and damages the impeller. On this alarm, stop the pump. Check the level in the suction vessel, check the suction line and the strainer for blockage, and restore the supply. Prime the pump again before restarting it, and find the cause of the loss before the pump is returned to service. The high bearing temperature alarm sounds when the bearing housing temperature rises above its set point. A hot bearing points to a lubrication fault or to an overloaded bearing, and continued running destroys the bearing. On this alarm, stop the pump and leave it stopped. Allow the bearings to cool. Check the oil level and the condition of the oil, and report the fault. Do not restart the pump until the cause has been found and cleared.

## Shutdown

Close the discharge valve gradually to bring the flow down, and stop the motor when the valve is nearly shut. Close the suction valve after the motor has stopped. A pump that is to stand idle is drained at the casing drain where the pumped liquid would set, corrode the internals, or freeze, and the drainings go to the drain system for the liquid concerned. Leave the pump full where it returns to service directly and the liquid is stable in the casing. Isolate the pump electrically and tag the starter before any work is done on it, and prove the isolation before the work starts. Record the shutdown in the log, with the state the pump is left in and any fault found during the running. The chapter covers the running of the pump: priming and starting, the readings and checks of normal operation, the two alarms and the action each one calls for, and the shutdown that leaves the pump stopped, isolated, and ready for work or for its next start.
